title: Steamboat Willie

evidence.note: Published 1928; the 95-year US copyright term expired and the film entered the public domain on January 1, 2024 — the most publicized Public Domain Day entry in history.
evidence.source: Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain — Public Domain Day 2024

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. § 101 defines 'motion picture' to include its accompanying sounds, and the Copyright Act treats a film's synchronized soundtrack as part of the single audiovisual work rather than a separate composition. On that basis the synchronized 1928 track shares the film's own copyright status.

Confirms the point is moot either way: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Motion Pictures, Jan-Dec 1956 (archive.org, searched directly): 'STEAMBOAT WILLIE, a motion picture in one reel by Walter E. Disney as employer for hire of U.B. Iwerks. (c) 21Nov28; M2124. Walt Disney Productions (PWH); 22Dec55; R162021.' Disney did renew in 1955, but a renewed 1928 work still tops out at the 95-year ceiling, which expired 1 January 2024 regardless — the same date Duke CSPD cites for the print.
evidence.source: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Motion Pictures, Jan-Dec 1956 (archive.org)

evidence.note: Plain note, no outside citation located for this specific claim: Steamboat Willie is an original 1928 short made for Disney by Ub Iwerks and Walt Disney; it adapts no earlier published book, play or comic, so there is no separate source work to clear. It shares the film print's own public-domain status above.

Disney holds live, actively enforced trademarks in Mickey Mouse names and imagery as brand identifiers. You may use the 1928 FILM and its specific character version creatively, but using Mickey as a logo, brand, or product identifier invites a trademark action. Later Mickey designs (gloves, color, modern proportions) remain copyrighted.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.
Disney's cleaned-up masters are separately protected; use archival scans.

editorial:
The 1928 short that built the Disney empire entered the public domain on January 1, 2024, after decades of copyright-term extensions nicknamed the 'Mickey Mouse Protection Act'. The film — including its synchronized whistling soundtrack — is free.

Mickey the BRAND is not. Disney's trademarks live on and are enforced: you can adapt the 1928 film and its scrappy, black-and-white Mickey creatively, but you cannot use Mickey as a logo, on packaging, or in ways that imply Disney origin. And only the 1928 design is free — the modern Mickey remains copyrighted. This is the clearest case on the internet of copyright and trademark pointing in opposite directions.
faq: Can I make and monetize a video using Steamboat Willie?
Yes — the 1928 film is public domain, including its soundtrack. Use archival scans, keep to the 1928 character design, and never present Mickey as your brand identifier.
Why did horror games and films start using Mickey in 2024?
Because the 1928 version's copyright expired — the same reason Winnie-the-Pooh horror appeared after 2022. Trademark law still polices branding, not creative reuse.
